summary: Preaching from Galatians 3:1-6, Steve confronts Paul's rebuke of the Galatians for turning from the gospel of faith back toward law-keeping. Three points: our faith saves us, not our own righteousness -- Paul asks them directly what actually caused them to receive the Spirit in the first place; justification happens the instant we believe (we immediately receive Christ's righteousness and the Holy Spirit) while sanctification is the lifelong, different-for-everyone process of being set apart that follows, worked out through obedience to Christ's three commands (love God, love others, make disciples) even through real failure; and freedom in Christ means we are no longer bound by the law. Steve also draws a practical distinction between the Holy Spirit's conviction (grace-rooted, moves us forward) and the enemy's condemnation (fear-rooted, dwells on the past), and names three steps for when we fail: confess it to God, redirect our focus back to Christ, and repent.
takeaways: Faith alone saves -- not personal righteousness or law-keeping; Paul asks the Galatians directly what actually caused them to receive the Spirit in the first place.

Justification happens the instant you believe -- you immediately receive Christ's righteousness and the Holy Spirit -- but sanctification is the lifelong process that follows, different for every believer, and never finished this side of death.
Real spiritual growth shows two ways at once: a growing hunger for God's word and a growing awareness of your own sin -- the more mature you get, the more you notice how far you have to go.

Conviction and condemnation can look similar but come from opposite places -- conviction is grace-rooted and moves you forward, condemnation is fear-rooted and dwells on the past. Know which one you're listening to.
Failure is part of sanctification, not proof you're not saved -- the response is the same three steps every time: confess it to God, redirect your focus back to Christ, and repent.
